solver.kind: blind AI solver B (separate agent, answer-free packet, adversarial rubric)

flags.note: C closely paraphrases the passage's 'not X but Y' framing (para 1 misconception vs. closing line), so it is easy to find by echo. A is the opposite view (the narrator's early mistaken belief); B and D inflate minor details (dialect, supervisor) into the main idea. No viable case for any distractor.

R050-01.notes: The arc runs from 'translation with pieces missing' to 'deciding what the viewer should keep.'

R050-02.notes: 'filled four lines, stayed on screen for less than five seconds... unreadable.' B is the reverse (he translated every insult). C misattributes: the speech was in dialect, not the subtitle. D confuses this with the pun anecdote. Choices are balanced in length.

R050-03.notes: 'doesn't need to know what she said... need to know that she won' means convey the outcome, not the content. A is the narrator's rejected approach. C contradicts 'she won.' B has no support.

flags.note: A has a slight foothold ('That remark changed how I thought'), but the paragraph is about reading versus watching, not a description of training. C overstates: 'much of the meaning,' not 'more than any dialogue.' C is the strongest distractor for careless readers.

R050-04.notes: 'Every word I add pulls the viewer's eyes away from the actors' faces... a viewer who is busy reading misses them.'

flags.note: B 'survives' is the common-meaning trap, but it does not fit 'where much of the meaning lives.' D 'is recorded' is weak. Only A works.

R050-05.notes: 'where much of the meaning lives' means where meaning is located, that is, 'is found.'

flags.note: D echoes the 'in-laws' detail as a word-echo trap, but the narrator's criterion is the same effect (the audience laughing 'at the same moment'), not the topic. B (shorter) conflicts with 'more than the dialogue contains.' C is a clean inference.

R050-06.notes: 'does the same work in the scene even though it says something else'; the test audience laughed at the same moment the original audience had.

flags.note: C deliberately swaps in the opposite case (the pun example from the same paragraph). It is a good distractor, not a defect.

R050-07.notes: '"Good morning" may be enough, because the warmth is in the actor's voice.'

flags.note: 'and so can tell what was cut' slightly overstates the passage. The passage says viewers know 'that I have made a choice' and 'can feel the difference,' not that they can identify what specifically was cut, which a viewer who doesn't know the source language could not do. Suggest 'can tell that something was cut' or 'can sense that choices were made.' It is still clearly the best answer.

R050-08.notes: 'A film's audience... hears the actors' real voices beneath every line.' A is the reverse, B distorts the test-audience detail, and C has no support.

flags.note: A could tempt readers because of 'I still lose things,' but the narrator rejects 'lesser kind of translation.' C is ruled out by 'I still lose things, of course.' D misreads the viewer noticing as a positive (honesty). B has the most text support.

R050-09.notes: 'I still lose things, of course. But I no longer think of my job as deciding what to throw away.'

flags.note: C repeats the passage's kept/lost wording almost verbatim, so it is somewhat cued by echo. The distractors are clearly wrong: A reverses the narrator's change, and B and D are unsupported.

R050-10.notes: 'I think of it as deciding what the viewer should keep' recasts the job in terms of what is kept.
